---
title: "The regression F statistic"
execute:
  enabled: true
  echo: true
  warning: false

---

The coefficient of determination tells us how much squared error the Provo line
removes relative to predicting every response by its sample mean. The
**regression $F$ statistic** asks how large that reduction is relative to the
residual variation expected under a Gaussian linear model.

This comparison uses two **nested models**. One model is nested within another
when the smaller model can be obtained by fixing one or more coefficients in the
larger model. Here the reduced model contains only an intercept, while the full
model adds modeled cloze surprisal:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal M_0:
Y_i
&=
\beta_0+\varepsilon_i, \\
\mathcal M_1:
Y_i
&=
\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\varepsilon_i.
\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $\beta_1=0$ in $\mathcal M_1$ recovers $\mathcal M_0$. We first derive
the comparison for $q$ restrictions, then calculate it for the one restriction
$\beta_1=0$ in the Provo regression.

## From two error sums to an F statistic

Let $\operatorname{SSE}_0$ be the squared error left by the reduced model and
$\operatorname{SSE}_1$ the squared error left by the full model. Because every
candidate available to the reduced model is also available to the full model,
least squares guarantees

$$
\operatorname{SSE}_1
\leq
\operatorname{SSE}_0.
$$

The difference

$$
\operatorname{SSE}_0-\operatorname{SSE}_1
$$

is the squared error removed by relaxing $q$ linearly independent restrictions.
Dividing by $q$ gives the removed squared error per independent restriction
relaxed. The full model's residual mean square is

$$
\frac{\operatorname{SSE}_1}{n-p},
$$

where $p$ counts the coefficients in the full model. The comparison is

$$
F
=
\frac{
(\operatorname{SSE}_0-\operatorname{SSE}_1)/q
}{
\operatorname{SSE}_1/(n-p)
}.
$$

Because the numerator and denominator have the same squared response unit,
their ratio has no unit. A value near one means that the removed error per
relaxed restriction is comparable to the residual error per remaining degree of
freedom; larger values indicate a greater reduction relative to that residual
scale.

Where does the reference distribution come from? A **full rank design** has $p$
predictor columns with no column equal to an exact weighted combination of the
others. The $q$ restrictions are **linearly independent** when none can be
obtained as a weighted combination of the rest. Suppose those conditions hold,
the errors are independent Gaussian random variables with common variance
$\sigma^2$, and the restrictions in the reduced model are true.

The [projection geometry](design-matrices.qmd#projection-as-fitted-plus-residual)
helps us see the next step. Think of the response as a vector with one
coordinate per observation. A **component** is the amount of that vector
pointing along a chosen direction. Moving from the reduced model to the full
model adds $q$ fitted directions. When the restrictions are true, the response
mean has no component in those directions; any observed improvement comes from
the Gaussian error vector. The full model residual occupies the $n-p$
directions perpendicular to every fitted direction. Thus the improvement and
the remaining residual error are squared lengths of perpendicular Gaussian
components.

As in the [chi-squared construction](../random-variables-and-distributions/chi-squared-distribution.qmd),
the squared length of $k$ independent standard normal components follows a
$\chi^2_k$ distribution. Perpendicular components of a Gaussian vector with
covariance $\sigma^2\mathbf I$ are independent. It follows that

$$
\frac{
\operatorname{SSE}_0-\operatorname{SSE}_1
}{\sigma^2}
\sim
\chi^2_q
$$

and

$$
\frac{\operatorname{SSE}_1}{\sigma^2}
\sim
\chi^2_{n-p}.
$$

The projection argument also gives the independence of these two quantities. An
**$F$ distribution** is the distribution of one independent chi-squared random
variable divided by its degrees of freedom, divided in turn by a second such
quantity. Thus

$$
F
\sim
F_{q,n-p}
$$

when the restrictions are true. The first subscript gives the numerator degrees
of freedom; the second gives the denominator degrees of freedom.

## Calculating the Provo F statistic

```{r}
#| label: calculate-provo-regression-f
library(ggplot2)

provo <- read.csv(
  "data/provo/content-word-positions.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
provo$cloze_surprisal_bits <- -log2(provo$OrthoMatchModel)

reduced_fit <- lm(mean_log_ffd ~ 1, data = provo)
full_fit <- lm(
  mean_log_ffd ~ cloze_surprisal_bits,
  data = provo
)

sse_reduced <- sum(residuals(reduced_fit)^2)
sse_full <- sum(residuals(full_fit)^2)
q <- length(coef(full_fit)) - length(coef(reduced_fit))
p <- length(coef(full_fit))
denominator_df <- nrow(provo) - p
removed_mean_square <- (sse_reduced - sse_full) / q
residual_mean_square <- sse_full / denominator_df
f_observed <- removed_mean_square / residual_mean_square
f_p_value <- pf(
  f_observed,
  df1 = q,
  df2 = denominator_df,
  lower.tail = FALSE
)

lm_f_output <- summary(full_fit)$fstatistic
stopifnot(
  abs(f_observed - unname(lm_f_output[["value"]])) < 1e-10,
  q == unname(lm_f_output[["numdf"]]),
  denominator_df == unname(lm_f_output[["dendf"]])
)

data.frame(
  reduced_sse = sse_reduced,
  full_sse = sse_full,
  restrictions = q,
  removed_mean_square = removed_mean_square,
  residual_mean_square = residual_mean_square,
  f_statistic = f_observed,
  numerator_degrees_of_freedom = q,
  denominator_degrees_of_freedom = denominator_df,
  p_value = f_p_value
)
```

Substituting the observed Provo sums of squares gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
F
&=
\frac{
(`r format(sse_reduced, digits = 7)`-
`r format(sse_full, digits = 7)`)/`r q`
}{
`r format(sse_full, digits = 7)`/`r denominator_df`
} \\
&=
`r format(f_observed, digits = 7)`.
\end{aligned}
$$

This direct calculation matches the `F-statistic` printed by
`summary(full_fit)`.

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-nested-fits
#| fig-cap: "Observed Provo position summaries with the reduced mean-only fit and the full fitted line."
grid <- data.frame(
  cloze_surprisal_bits = seq(
    min(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits),
    max(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits),
    length.out = 160L
  )
)
grid$full_fitted <- predict(full_fit, newdata = grid)
point_opacity <- 0.22

ggplot(provo, aes(cloze_surprisal_bits, mean_log_ffd)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey65", alpha = point_opacity, size = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = coef(reduced_fit)[["(Intercept)"]],
    color = "grey35",
    linetype = 2,
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid,
    aes(y = full_fitted),
    color = "#2C6E9B",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Modeled cloze surprisal (bits)",
    y = "Mean log first fixation duration"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The dashed line gives the reduced prediction and the blue line the full
prediction. Their vertical separation grows with modeled cloze surprisal, and
the $F$ calculation asks how much squared discrepancy the blue line removes.

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-f-reference
#| fig-cap: "Right-tail probability under a zero Provo slope. The point marks the F statistic and p value calculated from the observed data."
f_tail_grid <- data.frame(
  f = seq(0, f_observed * 1.08, length.out = 2001L)
)
f_tail_grid$right_tail_probability <- pf(
  f_tail_grid$f,
  df1 = q,
  df2 = denominator_df,
  lower.tail = FALSE
)

ggplot(f_tail_grid, aes(f, right_tail_probability)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey30", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = f_observed,
    color = "#B4473A",
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = data.frame(
      f = f_observed,
      right_tail_probability = f_p_value
    ),
    color = "#B4473A",
    size = 2
  ) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "F statistic", y = "Right-tail probability (log scale)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The right-tail probability is
`r format(f_p_value, scientific = TRUE, digits = 4)`. It describes how often a
null model with a zero slope would produce at least this much mean-square
improvement under the stated sampling assumptions.

## Why F equals t squared here

The current comparison relaxes one restriction, $\beta_1=0$. For a single
coefficient in an OLS model, the regression $F$ statistic equals the square of
the corresponding coefficient $t$ statistic:

$$
F_{1,n-p}=T_{n-p}^2.
$$

```{r}
#| label: verify-provo-f-equals-t-squared
slope_t <- coef(summary(full_fit))[
  "cloze_surprisal_bits",
  "t value"
]

stopifnot(abs(f_observed - slope_t^2) < 1e-10)

data.frame(
  slope_t_statistic = slope_t,
  squared_t_statistic = slope_t^2,
  regression_f_statistic = f_observed
)
```

The equality holds because both statistics compare the same one-dimensional
departure from $\beta_1=0$ with the same residual variance estimate. The $F$
form becomes more useful when a comparison relaxes several restrictions at
once, because it combines their reduction in SSE into one numerator mean
square.

A large $F$ value addresses only the restrictions that distinguish the reduced
and full models. Assessing the full linear specification requires [model
checks](checking-linear-regression.qmd). A causal interpretation additionally
requires an appropriate research design, while prediction for new passages
requires a declared [prediction target](../model-criticism-and-prediction/prediction-targets.qmd).

## Recap and check your understanding

1. What makes two regression models nested?
2. What does the numerator mean square measure?
3. Which assumptions give the exact $F_{q,n-p}$ reference distribution?
4. Why does $F=T^2$ for the current comparison?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The reduced model can be obtained by fixing one or more coefficients in the full model. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. It measures the reduction in squared error per restriction relaxed when moving from the reduced model to the full model. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Independent Gaussian errors with a common conditional variance, together with true reduced-model restrictions, give the exact finite sample distribution. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The comparison tests one slope restriction with the same residual variance estimate used by the slope $t$ statistic. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>

We next examine whether the fitted line's restrictions agree with the observed
[residual patterns](checking-linear-regression.qmd).
